title: Double check: how to see it, set it up and stop it
outcomes: Explains why only the king can answer a double check, and when the king may capture a checking piece
Finds the move that gives a double check by looking for a piece that stands in front of a line to the king
Says that a move is no double check when a piece blocks the uncovered line or the front piece gives no check
Sets up a double check with a first forcing move and spots one aimed at their own king
Explains double check to a beginner with the idea, its conditions, an example and a warning

steps.prompt: Write the move you chose, and what you think could stop it. Nothing is explained yet.

steps.text: **Double check** means one move gives check twice, so the king has to move. After this lesson you can do four things: **see** one coming, **judge** whether it works (and when the king simply takes the checking piece), **set one up** or stop one against you, and **tell** a real double check from a look-alike. First, boards from easy to hard: watch what the first move does.

steps.text: **Two pieces on one line.** Every board had the same parts. A *back piece* (a queen, rook or bishop) aims at the king along a line, and a *front piece* stands in the way. When the front piece moves, the back piece gives check. If the front piece also gives check from its new square, that is a **double check**. So the search is: find a piece standing between your long-range piece and the enemy king.

steps.chapter: Why it works, and when it fails

line.say: Only the king can move. Capturing or blocking one checker would leave the other check standing.

steps.text: **Why only the king can answer.** A single check can be met three ways: take the checking piece, block the line, or move the king. A capture or a block deals with one checker, and the other check is still there. So the king must move. That includes the king *capturing* a checker, if the checker stands next to the king and nothing protects it.

options: whenever it is a minor piece

fields.answer: only if no white piece attacks that square, the other checker included

steps.text: **What a double check needs, and what makes it win.** It needs an open line once the front piece leaves, and a front piece that checks from its new square. Miss either and you have one check, which can be blocked or captured. It wins when the king cannot take the checker and every flight square is covered. Even then the forced king move buys a free move, because the king had to answer. That free move can bring mate, a fork or an undefended piece.

steps.text: **Which piece moves in front? [V] our data.** In 39 Lichess puzzles (CC0, chosen for the double-check theme, so not a fair sample of games) whose key move is a true double check, the front piece was a knight 25 times, a pawn 8, a rook 4, a bishop 2, and never a queen or king in this sample. A knight always checks from two squares away, so the king can never take it (geometry). [H] That may explain why knights lead the count.

steps.text: **Setting one up, and stopping one.** [I] Two ways to set one up, from the boards in this lesson: put a long-range piece behind a piece that has a checking square, or use a first check to drive the king onto the line. Dan Heisman advises listing the opponent's checks, captures and threats before each move [S, paraphrased]. [I] The question this theme adds: does an enemy long-range piece stand behind a piece that could check my king?

steps.text: **Many defences work.** [V] At depth 16 the engine rates stepping the king off the rank, advancing a pawn and capturing with the rook within about a pawn of each other. What fails is leaving the king on the line. [I] So ask before each move: does an enemy long-range piece stand behind a piece that could check me? The king, the back piece or the front piece can move, or the line can be blocked.

**Two look-alikes and one failed double check.** (1) The line is blocked, so the move gives one check. (2) The front piece lands where it does not attack the king: a *discovered* check, which can be blocked. And a real double check can still fail: the king takes the checker, or has a safe square (the third condition). Ask: which check is missing, or which king answer exists?

steps.text: **What others say.** Nimzowitsch (*My System*, chapter on discovered check) describes double check as leaving the king nothing but flight, and calls it purely tactical [V-sheet: paraphrased from our own notes, not the book page]. Jacob Aagaard argues that many calculation errors start with a candidate move that was never considered [S, a reviewer's account, paraphrased]. [I] So the habit: put the double check on your candidate list before you calculate.

**What to remember.**
1. Double check: two checkers, so only the king can move.
2. A back piece, a front piece, an open line.
3. The front piece must check from where it lands.
4. The king may take a checker next to it, if nothing covers that square.
5. Count the flight squares: mate, or a free move.
6. Look-alikes: blocked line, or no front check.
7. Defence: ask what long-range piece stands behind a piece that could check you. Move the king or either piece.

steps.prompt: Teach a beginner. Write four things: what a double check is, when it works, an example they could set up on a board (pieces and squares), and one warning. Self-check, nothing is graded: did you say why only the king can answer, name one condition that can fail, and give a look-alike?

A model answer [I], in the author's words. Idea: one move makes two pieces check at once, so only the king can answer. When it works: the line is open, the front piece checks where it lands, and the king cannot take the checker or reach a safe square. Example: White rook e1, bishop e5, pawn c5, Black king e7; the bishop to d6 is mate. Warning: without the pawn on c5 the king takes the bishop. Compare with yours.
